1. Introduction
The global push to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and address
climate change has made electric vehicles (EVs) a critical technol-
ogy for sustainable transportation. In the past decade, the adop-
tion of EVs has increased exponentially driven by advancements
in battery management system (BMS), battery technologies,
government
incentives,
and
increasing
environmental awareness. Recent advances
in power electronics, charging techniques,
and real-time control systems have focu-
sed on enhancing the management of
battery behavior, addressing environmental
impacts, and improving efﬁciency in EVs,
as these developments are crucial for
advancing sustainable transportation solu-

tinuous innovations in battery systems
and vehicle technologies. The BMS plays
an essential role in ensuring the reliability,

and managing battery operations to opti-
mize performance.[3] Lithium-ion batteries
(LIBs)
have
become
the
predominant

This is attributed to their high energy den-
sity, superior speciﬁc energy, and comparatively lower cost.[4,5]
However, advancements in LIBs and next-generation technolo-
gies such as solid-state batteries (SSBs) and lithium-metal batter-
ies (LMBs) continue to progress.[6] The focus shifts toward
leveraging BMS to address their inherent limitations and ensure
efﬁcient, safe, and long-lasting use in EVs.
The BMS is an electronic system designed to monitor and con-
trol the performance of batteries or battery packs. It ensures safe,
efﬁcient, and reliable operation of an EV. Its primary functions
include performance management, thermal protection, state esti-
mation, fault diagnosis, and communication for data storage and
transmission.[7] These functions are critical to extend battery life,
improve reliability, and ensure safety in EV applications. State
estimation monitors key parameters such as state of charge
(SoC), state of health (SoH), and remaining useful life (RUL),
enabling efﬁcient energy management and early fault detection.
Thermal management maintains battery temperature within safe
limits to prevent overheating and ensure longevity. Fault diagno-
sis ensures safety by detecting and addressing issues like sensor
faults, actuator errors, and cell inconsistencies before they esca-
late. Figure 2 provides a comprehensive depiction of the BMS
structure and its core functionalities within an electric vehicle.

Electric vehicles (EVs) are pivotal in the global transition toward sustainable
transportation with lithium-ion batteries and battery management systems
(BMS) play critical roles in safety, efﬁciency, and reliability. This review
synthesizes advancements in battery technologies and BMS functionalities,
highlighting challenges such as thermal management, state estimation, cell
balancing, and fault diagnosis. It explores emerging battery chemistries including
solid-state and sodium-ion batteries, thermal regulation techniques, preheating
strategies, recycling methods, second-life applications, and advanced energy
recovery systems examined for their potential to enhance battery performance
and lifecycle sustainability. The integration of cutting-edge technologies, such as
artiﬁcial intelligence, digital twins, cloud computing, blockchain, Internet of
Things, and advanced data analytics, is revolutionizing BMS capabilities. These
technologies enable high-precision monitoring, predictive analytics, and opti-
mized energy management, enabling integration of EVs into complex energy
networks through vehicle-to-grid, vehicle-to-home, and smart grid systems. By
synthesizing current research and identifying critical gaps, this paper guides the
development of EV technologies. It underscores the signiﬁcant contributions of
integrating advanced technologies into BMS and clariﬁes the extensive beneﬁts
of such advancements. The methodologies and ﬁndings of the study are poised
to enhance energy sustainability and efﬁciency, setting a benchmark for future
advancements in the ﬁeld.

In addition to advancements in BMS technologies, progress in
battery innovations is crucial to accelerate EV adoption. LIBs
dominate the electric vehicle (EV) market because of their high
energy density and affordability. However, ongoing technological
advancements are aimed to overcome their existing limita-
tions.[15] The SSBs and LMBs are emerging as promising alter-
natives that offer improved safety and higher energy densities.[6]
Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) provide a cost-effective and environ-
mentally friendly solution with comparable performance met-
rics.[6] As EV production scales up, battery recycling and
second-life applications such as repurposing used batteries for
grid storage are vital to ensure sustainability.[16] Innovative
approaches such as wireless power transfer (WPT) and battery
swapping are being adopted to address energy refueling chal-
lenges particularly for public transport, reducing downtime
and improving operational efﬁciency.[17] When combined with
advancements in charging infrastructure, these innovations
have the potential to signiﬁcantly accelerate the global adoption
of EVs.
Advancements in BMS and battery technologies are essential
for the continued growth and adoption of EVs. AI-based techni-
ques, cloud computing, and blockchain integration will drive
the future of BMS helping to ensure the safety, reliability, and
efﬁciency of EV batteries.[12,18] These advancements will play a
critical role in meeting future energy demands and contributing
to global sustainability goals.
This review is motivated by the observation that while the
existing literature on BMS in EVs covers various aspects, it often
lacks a comprehensive integration of recent advancements, prac-
tical applications, and future directions. Recognizing this gap,
our paper aims to provide a holistic overview, addressing both
current technologies and emerging trends. The contributions
of this paper are structured as follows:
Battery technology assessment: Extensive evaluation of various
battery technologies including prelithium, lithium-based, and
postlithium options, and their impact on EV performance.
Battery modeling review: Systematic review of battery modeling
and state estimation approaches, covering common battery mod-
els and estimation techniques for critical states such as SoC,
SoH, and RUL.
BMS functional analysis: Detailed examination of key BMS
functionalities such as status estimation methods, battery cell
balancing, fault diagnosis, and thermal management.
Integration of AI in BMS: Exploration of AI-based techniques
for enhancing the predictive capabilities and overall efﬁciency of
battery management systems.
Challenges and future research directions: Identiﬁcation of cur-
rent challenges and barriers in BMS technologies, proposal of
future research directions, and provision of a comprehensive
resource for advancing battery management in EVs.
2. Battery Types and Technologies
The automotive industry’s transition to electric mobility places
energy storage advancements at the forefront. These advance-
ments play a critical role in improving the performance, range,
and safety of EVs. This section provides a comprehensive
examination of various energy storage solutions particularly
focusing on batteries while also considering supercapacitors
and fuel cells. The unique characteristics, beneﬁts, and limita-
tions of each technology will be explored to provide a detailed
understanding of their contributions to current and future EV
designs.
2.1. Advancements and Innovations in Battery Technologies
The advancement of battery technologies has been pivotal in sup-
porting the transition to electric mobility. Batteries are classiﬁed
into various types based on their chemistry, design, and applica-
tions. Each type offers distinct performance characteristics and
limitations. The evolution of battery technologies, from early
lead-acid systems to modern lithium-based solutions, highlights
signiﬁcant progress. Emerging innovations such as metal-air and
sodium-based batteries also hold great potential to address the
energy storage challenges of EVs.
2.1.1. Classiﬁcation of Batteries
Batteries are classiﬁed into two main types: primary (nonre-
chargeable) and secondary (rechargeable) batteries. The EV sec-
tor predominantly relies on secondary batteries because of their
ability to endure numerous charge–discharge cycles. This makes
them both economically viable and environmentally sustain-
able.[19] Historically, lead-acid batteries were the ﬁrst choice in
early EV models. However, their limitations including low spe-
ciﬁc energy and short lifecycle have necessitated a shift toward
advanced battery technologies.[20] The evolution from lead-acid
systems to modern lithium-based solutions has marked signiﬁ-
cant progress in energy storage capabilities. Emerging innova-
tions, such as metal-air and sodium-based batteries, hold
promise for addressing energy storage challenges and improving
the range, safety, and performance of EVs. Figure 3 illustrates the
classiﬁcation of energy storage systems (ESS) relevant to EVs
highlighting key categories such as ultracapacitors, electrochem-
ical batteries, and fuel cells, along with their speciﬁc subtypes. By
understanding these developments, researchers and engineers
can further optimize energy storage solutions to meet the grow-
ing demands of electric mobility.
2.1.2. Historical Context of Prelithium Batteries
Lead-Acid Batteries: Lead-acid batteries were ﬁrst developed in the
1800s and have maintained a long-standing presence in the auto-
motive market. Although reliable, their low speciﬁc energy of
≈40 Wh kg1 and limited energy density of around 90 Wh L1
increasingly render them unsuitable for modern electric vehicle
applications.[21,22] Their use is primarily relegated to traditional
vehicles for functions like starting and lighting as the market
moves toward more efﬁcient solutions.
Nickel-Based Technologies: Nickel-based batteries, speciﬁcally
nickel-metal hydride (Ni-MH) and nickel-cadmium (Ni-Cd),
emerged in the 1990s as potential successors to lead-acid
systems. Ni-MH batteries offered signiﬁcant enhancements in
both energy density and lifecycle thus serving as a viable option
for early hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs).[23] Nonetheless, the

2.1.3. Advancements in Lithium-Based Batteries
Lithium-Ion Batteries: Since their introduction in 1991, LIBs have
fundamentally transformed the energy storage landscape for
EVs. They are characterized by high speciﬁc energy (ranging
from 150 to 250 Wh kg1) and superior energy density (between
300 and 900 Wh L1).[24] The efﬁcient charge and discharge capa-
bilities of LIBs result in extended operational lifetimes. Ongoing
research focuses on improving their thermal stability and charg-
ing rates to reduce safety risks.[25]
Lithium-Metal Batteries: Lithium-metal batteries (LMBs) repre-
sent a cutting-edge advancement within the lithium family. They
offer exceptional speciﬁc capacities of up to 3860 mAh g1 by
utilizing metallic lithium anodes.[26] Despite their potential, den-
drite formation during cycling poses signiﬁcant safety challenges
for LMBs. Innovative solutions are required to address these
issues and fully leverage the advantages of LMBs while ensuring
safe operation.
2.1.4. Next-Generation Battery Technologies
The quest for sustainable high-performance batteries has
sparked interest in postlithium technologies including metal/
air and sodium-based batteries.
Metal-Air Battery Systems: Metal-air batteries, particularly
lithium-air and zinc-air variants, offer exciting prospects with
their theoretical speciﬁc energies (up to 11 700 Wh kg1 for
lithium-air).[27,28] These systems utilize atmospheric oxygen as
a cathode material which has the potential to enable lighter
and more energy-dense conﬁgurations. However, their practical
implementation is limited by challenges such as electrolyte sta-
bility and air management. These issues necessitate further
research before the technology can be applied to commercial
electric vehicle applications.
Sodium-Based Batteries: Sodium-ion batteries are emerging
as a competitive alternative to lithium technologies offer-
ing beneﬁts such as abundant resources and lower costs.
Sodium-beta (ZEBRA) batteries have shown notable perfor-
mance,

environments.
However, their speciﬁc energy levels remain lower than those
of LIBs.[29,30]
2.1.5. Flow Battery Technology
Flow batteries, which can be categorized into redox-ﬂow and
hybrid systems, offer a distinctive approach to energy storage.
Their design enables independent scaling of energy and power
capacities through the external storage of electrolytes.[31,32]
Although this ﬂexibility allows for prolonged lifetimes, their
lower energy density continues to pose challenges for applica-
tions in portable electronics.[33,34]

2.2. Supercapacitors
Supercapacitors are also known as ultracapacitors and provide
an alternative energy storage solution that is characterized by
high power density and rapid charge-discharge capabilities.
Their energy density is signiﬁcantly lower than that of batteries
which makes them unsuitable for long-term energy storage
applications. However, they are highly effective in scenarios
that require quick power bursts such as regenerative braking
systems.[33,34] The combination of supercapacitors and batteries
in hybrid energy storage systems (HESS) can effectively provide
a balance between sustained energy output and rapid power
delivery.

2.3. Fuel Cells
Fuel cells are electrochemical devices that generate electricity by
combining hydrogen and oxygen, producing water as the only
emission. This technology has the potential to deliver extended
driving ranges and facilitate quick refueling compared to tradi-
tional battery systems.[35,36] However, the widespread adoption
of fuel cells in passenger vehicles is limited by factors such as
high costs, infrastructure demands, and energy conversion
efﬁciency.[37,38]
2.4. Future Directions in Hybrid System
The future landscape of energy storage in EVs is likely to feature
hybrid systems that integrate multiple technologies to optimize
performance across various parameters. By harnessing the com-
plementary strengths of batteries, supercapacitors, and fuel cells,
manufacturers can engineer vehicles with enhanced range and
efﬁciency.[39] The ongoing research focuses on improving the
energy density, lifecycle, and safety proﬁles of current technolo-
gies while exploring new materials and conﬁgurations to meet
the evolving demands of electric mobility.
3. Battery Modeling
Battery modeling is essential to predict and optimize ESS perfor-
mance. It also plays a critical role in ensuring their efﬁciency
safety and longevity particularly in electric vehicles. Battery mod-
els are typically categorized into three types. Electrochemical
models (EMs) represent internal processes using complex equa-
tions. Electrical equivalent circuit models (ECMs) approximate
battery
behavior
through
components
like
resistors
and
capacitors. Data-driven models rely on AI algorithms, such as
neural networks (NN) and support vector machines (SVM) to pre-
dict performance without requiring detailed internal knowledge.
These models are vital for estimating critical parameters such
as SoC and SoH. This enhances BMS while improving
energy efﬁciency and durability in sustainable applications.
Ultimately, the goal of battery models is to create reliable,
long-lasting, and efﬁcient ESS for sustainable technologies.
Each type of model offers distinct advantages and limitations.
These aspects will be examined in detail in the following
sections.
3.1. Electrochemical Models
EMs describe battery behavior through partial differential equa-
tions (PDEs) that account for factors such as electrolyte concen-
tration, electrode size, and electrochemical processes. These
models exhibit a high degree of accuracy. However, their compu-
tational demands pose signiﬁcant challenges for implementation
in real-time applications. Simpliﬁed models address this limita-
tion by focusing on key variables such as diffusion and electrolyte
concentration, providing greater computational efﬁciency at the
cost of reduced accuracy.[40] One such simpliﬁed approach is
the Single-Particle (SP) model, where a single particle is used
to represent lithium-ion concentration distribution within the
electrode. While this model effectively analyzes the primary per-
formance and solid-phase diffusion effects, it suffers from
reduced accuracy.[41] An enhanced Single Particle Model with
Electrolyte dynamics (SPMe) incorporates the inﬂuence of the
electrolyte on the output voltage. It improves simulation accuracy
by introducing additional PDEs to describe material conservation
and charge distribution within the electrolyte thus addressing the
limitations of the standard SP model.[42]
The Pseudo-2-D (P2D) model known for its high ﬁdelity rep-
resents the anode and cathode as porous electrodes ﬁlled with
electrolyte and describes the concentration and potential distri-
bution of lithium ions in both solid and liquid phases using cou-
pled
PDEs.

3.2. Equivalent Circuit Models
ECM simulates battery electrical behavior using components
such as resistors, capacitors, and voltage sources. A high-value
capacitor or a regulated voltage source is commonly used to rep-
resent the open-circuit voltage (OCV) which is a crucial parame-
ter for state estimation approaches in BMS.[52] Among the
simplest ECMs is the Rint model, which models the battery
as a voltage source in series with resistance. However, this model
does not capture the detailed dynamics of batteries used in EVs.
To improve the model’s representation of battery behavior, the
Thevenin model incorporates a resistance-capacitance (RC) par-
allel network which provides more accurate predictions of battery
behavior.[53]
The Rint model, as depicted in Figure 4a, represents the bat-
tery with a voltage source Voc in series with an internal resistance
R0. This simple conﬁguration is effective for estimating the
OCV and overall internal resistance. However, it fails to capture
the dynamic response of batteries under varying conditions.
Figure 4b presents an enhanced model with RC networks, where
the resistors represent different internal resistances and capaci-
tors account for charge storage. This conﬁguration captures
short-term dynamic behavior and transient responses making
it suitable for modeling batteries during rapid changes in load.
The Thevenin model, shown in Figure 4c, integrates an RC net-
work (R1, C1) with the internal resistance R0. This enhancement
enables the model to more accurately simulate transient voltage
behavior, particularly during charging and discharging cycles.
This is achieved by accounting for the time-dependent voltage
decay associated with capacitive elements. Finally, Figure 4d
illustrates an extended RC network model that includes an addi-
tional RC branch (R0, C0). This conﬁguration improves the repre-
sentation of battery dynamics across a wide frequency range. It
enables a comprehensive analysis of both transient and steady-
state performance under varying operational conditions.
The partnership for a new generation of vehicles (PNGV)
model, a variation of the Thevenin model, adds a ﬁctive capacitor
to account for OCV variations. Although this model performs
well in low SoC regions, it is less accurate in high SoC areas.[54]
RC network-based models have gained popularity due to their
enhanced ability to model battery dynamics. Variants such as
the one RC network, two RC network, and three RC network
models have been widely used in real-time application. The

accurately simulate both ionic and electronic transport processes.
This conﬁguration is particularly valuable for high-ﬁdelity analy-
sis of battery performance. It is especially useful when detailed
electrochemical and thermal dynamics are required.
Batteries are nonlinear systems, and their behavior changes
with factors such as SoC, temperature, and charge or discharge
rates.[55,56] These variations create challenges in parameter iden-
tiﬁcation and optimization. To align the model with measured
data, parameters must be carefully updated to reﬂect these fac-
tors. Accurate parameterization requires thorough consideration
of SoC, temperature, and charge or discharge rates. This ensures
reliability and optimal performance in real-world applications.
3.3. Data-Driven Models
Data-driven models (DDMs) offer an efﬁcient alternative to ECM
and EMs for approximating highly nonlinear battery behaviors.
Unlike ECMs and EMs, which require detailed knowledge of
the battery’s internal structure, DDMs rely on data-driven
approaches and computational intelligence to model battery
dynamics. These models are particularly useful when a global
mathematical model of the system is unavailable or difﬁcult to
derive. Table 3 provides a summary of various data-driven model-

recurrent neural networks (RNN).[61] These methods are widely
applied for SoC and SoH estimation, offering effective solutions
for battery performance modeling.
DDMs provide several advantages, including the ability to han-

instance, feedforward neural networks (FFNN), which use gradi-

ability to handle temporal sequences limiting their effectiveness
in SoC estimation.[62] DNNs and LSTM-RNNs (long short-term
memory-RNN), on the other hand, are better suited for capturing
intricate temporal dependencies, with the latter excelling at learn-

4.2. Model-Based Methods for Battery State Estimation
Model-based techniques are widely used to estimate key battery
parameters, including SoH, SoT, SoC, and RUL. Figure 7 depicts
the general framework of the model-based state estimation
method. The Kalman ﬁlter (KF) is a prominent method that is
known for its ability to reduce noise and manage uncertainty.
Adaptive extended KF methods have been developed to handle
distribution changes and improve accuracy.[81] An adaptive
square-root extended KF incorporating a Thevenin ECM was val-
idated under dynamic temperature conditions to address ﬁltering
divergence.[82] Additionally, an adaptive cubature KF has been
introduced to improve generalization and reduce design com-
plexity.[83] To address estimator deviation over time, adaptive
unscented KF techniques refresh noise covariance for more reli-
able SoH and RUL estimations.[84] KF-based thermal models
have also been used to predict both surface and internal temper-
atures without additional sensors.[85] New methods like the
fading Kalman ﬁlter (FKF), which incorporates fading factors
to correct modeling errors, offer improved accuracy for dynamic
battery behavior. This approach balances real-time estimation
with computational efﬁciency.[86]
The particle ﬁlter (PF) is effective in nonlinear and non-
Gaussian conditions, using a Monte Carlo method to estimate
battery states by modeling the relationship between SoC, current,
and voltage ﬂuctuations.[87] Advanced PF methods, including a
gradient-correction PF for LIB aging trajectories and a novel
extended Kalman PF, have been proposed to enhance RUL pre-
dictions.[82] Multimodel PFs and second-order central difference
PFs have further improved capacity and RUL estimations while
reducing uncertainty.
The observer-based methods provide an alternative, relying on
real-time feedback. proportional-integral observers (PIOs) efﬁ-
ciently estimate SoC by addressing system uncertainties.[88]
Fractional-order estimators, such as Luenberger and sliding
mode observers, improve robustness and accuracy under uncer-
tain conditions.[89,90] The H∞observer method is another
model-based approach that manages uncertainties effectively
by optimizing gain for noise and modeling errors. Though com-
putationally demanding, it ensures robust state estimation in
highly dynamic systems.[91] H∞observers, using fractional-order
ECMs, have been applied to SoC estimation through electro-
chemical impedance analysis.[92] Other nonlinear observers are
explored to minimize estimation errors and enhance system
robustness.[93]

acteristics using techniques such as regression, classiﬁcation,
and dimensionality reduction. These methods are particularly
advantageous for addressing challenges faced by traditional
approaches, such as ECM or EM, when dealing with the
complexity and variability of battery systems. With their high

5. Safety Issues and Fault Diagnosis
5.1. Thermal Management
Thermal management is crucial for ensuring the safety and per-
formance of LIBs in EVs. Operating batteries outside their opti-
mal temperature range of 20–40 °C can degrade capacity, shorten
lifespan, and lead to dangerous events like thermal runaway.[115]
Low temperatures may cause the formation of lithium dendrite
that leads to short circuits and increased internal resistance,
while high temperatures can cause combustion or explo-
sions.[116] Figure 9 illustrates the progression of thermal runaway
in LIBs, describing the stages from a stable operating state to
catastrophic failure. Under normal conditions, the battery main-
tains a balance between heat generation (Hg) and dissipation
(Hd), ensuring thermal stability. However, triggering events such
as excessive heat, mechanical damage, overcharging, or internal/
external short circuits can disrupt this balance, leading to
increased heat generation. This results in a temperature rise that
accelerates reaction rates, creating a self-sustaining feedback loop
known as thermal runaway. Potential hazards include smoke,
ﬁre, explosions, toxic gas release, and the propagation of thermal
runaway to adjacent cells, emphasizing the critical importance of
effective thermal management strategies.

5.1.1. Internal Modiﬁcations
Internal modiﬁcations focus on improving the structural
and material properties of the battery to enhance thermal perfor-
mance.[117] These modiﬁcations include adjusting the thickness
of electrodes to improve thermal dissipation and employing
various material enhancement techniques, such as optimizing
particle size, applying surface coatings, incorporating doping
materials, adding thermal additives, and using deposition tech-
niques to enhance heat transfer within battery cells.
5.1.2. External Systems
External systems are designed to manage the heat generated
within the battery pack by employing external cooling or heating
mechanisms. They provide a reliable means of maintaining the
battery’s thermal stability, which is essential to ensure safety,
prolong lifespan, and achieve optimal performance under
varying operational conditions. Three primary types of external
systems are active cooling, passive cooling, and hybrid cooling
and are discussed in the following sections.
Active Cooling: Active cooling methods, such as liquid cooling
and air cooling, are widely used to regulate battery temperature.
Liquid cooling techniques include direct immersion, liquid jack-
ets, cold plates, and advanced methods such as mini/micro ser-
pentine channels. These systems, while effective, require
external components like fans and pumps, leading to increased
energy consumption and design complexity.[118–120] Recent
advances, such as minichannel cold plates have improved cooling
performance, particularly under high discharge rates, though
they come with higher power consumption. Another promising
approach is thermoelectric cooling, which uses solid-state com-
ponents to transfer heat efﬁciently.[121]
Passive Cooling: Passive cooling methods, such as phase
change materials (PCMs), are gaining popularity due to their
ability to absorb and release latent heat without external energy
input.[122,123] Pure PCMs provide basic thermal regulation, while
composite PCMs offer enhanced performance. Advances in
PCM technology, such as adding expanded graphite (EG) and
metal nanoparticles, have signiﬁcantly improved heat dissipa-
tion.[124,125] Heat pipe-based cooling, which combines PCMs
with heat pipes for improved heat transport, is also an emerging
solution. Composite PCMs, such as those incorporating parafﬁn
wax with polymers,[126] EG, and metal nanoparticles, have dem-
onstrated excellent thermal stability and conductivity, making
them suitable for high-performance battery systems.[127]
Hybrid Cooling: Hybrid systems combining liquid cooling with
PCMs have shown promise in improving cooling efﬁciency and
reducing costs.[122] More advanced hybrid approaches, such as
PCM combined with air cooling, PCM combined with liquid
cooling, and PCM integrated with heat pipes, provide better
thermal regulation by leveraging the strengths of both active
and passive methods. Additionally, heat pipe combined with
air cooling and heat pipe integrated with liquid cooling further
enhance performance by optimizing heat transfer pathways.
5.1.3. Preheating
At low temperatures, preheating systems are essential for warm-
ing batteries to their optimal operating range before charging or
discharging, thereby preventing issues such as lithium plating
and increased internal resistance that compromise performance
and safety.[128,129] Common techniques include internal heating,
where resistive heaters embedded in battery modules generate
heat.[130] External heating methods, such as heat pumps or heat-
ing pads, are used to raise the battery temperature.[131]
Additionally, self-heating methods leverage battery currents to
produce heat internally, reducing the need for external compo-
nents. The preheating systems are particularly crucial in cold cli-
mates, as they enhance charge acceptance, prevent dendrite
formation, and extend battery life.

5.2. Cell Balancing
Cell balancing methods are generally classiﬁed into two catego-
ries: passive and active balancing. Figure 11 illustrates the
approach of active and passive cell balancing in an EV battery
pack, emphasizing their distinct methods of managing energy
and ensuring safety. The passive balancing utilizes a simple
resistive circuit to dissipate excess energy from overcharged cells.
This approach is straightforward, but it suffers from low
efﬁciency and generates additional heat.[133] In contrast, active
balancing redistributes energy from overcharged cells to under-
charged ones using advanced circuitry, minimizing energy loss
and providing better system efﬁciency. On the other hand, active
balancing redistributes energy dynamically to promote uniform
charge levels and extend overall battery performance and
lifespan.[134]
Cell balancing is a critical aspect of battery management in
EVs as inconsistencies in manufacturing and chemical reactions
can cause variations in cell voltage, SoC, capacity fade rate, and
aging rate.[135] These disparities can lead to severe issues such as
leakage, explosions, or ﬁres, particularly when some cells become
overcharged or discharged. Therefore, maintaining voltage
equalization across all cells in a battery pack is essential for both
safety and performance.
Recent advancements in active balancing technologies include
the development of switched-capacitor circuits and modular
architectures that reduce energy loss and improve overall system
stability.[136] Symmetrical switched-capacitor structures have
been optimized to provide faster voltage equalization by
maximizing current paths, ensuring quicker response times
and better balancing across cells.[137] In addition to hardware
improvements, the software and algorithms controlling cell bal-
ancing play a crucial role in optimizing performance. Commonly
used algorithms focus on three primary objectives: voltage uni-
formity, capacity uniformity, and SoC uniformity.[138,139] These
algorithms are designed to maintain a consistent charge and dis-
charge proﬁle across all cells, preventing overloading of weaker
cells and ensuring the longevity of the battery pack.

Qualitative methods, like graph theory and expert systems,
rely on observed system behaviors and prior knowledge, making

Model-based methods, on the other hand, use mathematical
models of battery systems to compare actual versus predicted
behavior, detecting faults with high accuracy, including short

6. Emerging Technologies in Safety
The evolution of EV battery management now includes advanced
safety measures via DT and blockchain technology. The DTs and
predictive maintenance offer real-time virtual replicas for
continuous monitoring and diagnostics, addressing issues like
overheating and degradation early on, and enabling proactive
maintenance, thus extending battery life and enhancing reliabil-
ity.[156] Blockchain and cloud technologies further enhance data
security and transparency, providing tamper-proof, traceable data
management and real-time analytics.[157] These advancements
foster a safer, more efﬁcient approach to EV battery manage-
ment, supporting sustainability and reliability. The following sec-
tions will delve deeper into these technologies and their impacts
on EV battery systems.
6.1. Digital Twin and Predictive Maintenance Using AI
The Digital Twin technology in BMS leverages cloud-based
computational power to achieve high-precision estimations for
critical battery parameters, like SoC and SoH, surpassing the lim-
itations of traditional onboard BMS processors.[158] DTs enable
real-time monitoring, diagnostics, and predictive maintenance,
using extensive data on voltage, current, and temperature trans-
mitted through protocols like CAN and MQTT. For instance,
studies have shown DTs achieving MAE as low as 0.49% for
SoC estimation using advanced adaptive H∞ﬁlters and particle
swarm optimization.[153] Further improvements in DT applica-
tions incorporate LSTM networks to estimate battery capacity
with an MAE of 2.86%, adapting to reﬂect battery aging effects
over time.[159] DTs also support precise cell balancing by forecast-
ing balancing requirements and implementing control strate-
gies,
attaining
SoC
and
SoH
MAEs
of
0.3
and
0.5%,
respectively.[152] Advanced techniques, including KF, least-
squares SVM, and ML algorithms such as random forest,
gradient boosting, and DNN, continue to reﬁne DT accuracy
in real-time battery diagnostics.[160–163] DTs can also be inte-
grated into cloud-based BMS architectures, sometimes used
interchangeably with predictive DTs when focused on real-time
monitoring and predictive capabilities for battery health and
safety.[164]
6.2. Blockchain Technology
Blockchain technology offers signiﬁcant advancements for BMS
by enabling decentralized, transparent, and secure management
of essential battery parameters such as SoC and SoH. In
ref. [165], an overview is presented for blockchain applications
in sustainable energy, outlining potential scenarios where block-
chain enhances data integrity and energy management. A
broader survey in[166] extends blockchain and IoT applications
to the industrial sector, covering autonomous vehicle data man-
agement, supply chain tracking, and asset monitoring in
manufacturing, all of which are relevant to the extensive data
demands in EV BMS.
For EV BMS speciﬁcally, Ethereum’s smart contracts auto-
mate key transactions, securing data sharing across EV net-
works,[167] charging stations, and battery swap systems without
requiring intermediaries. However, Ethereum’s high transaction
fees can limit scalability in data-intensive contexts. IOTA, which
uses a directed acyclic graph (DAG) structure instead of a linear
blockchain, facilitates fee-free transactions, making it particularly
suitable for real-time IoT data sharing in EV BMS.[168] The effec-
tive use of IOTA for integrating IoT devices, creating a decentral-
ized platform for data sharing, and supporting battery state
monitoring and peer-to-peer energy exchange was examined
in recent studies. By integrating both Ethereum’s and IOTA’s
strengths, EV BMS systems can achieve a scalable, secure data
infrastructure that supports high-frequency, decentralized man-
agement essential for sustainable EV operations.
Integrating DT and blockchain technologies in BMS enhances
real-time monitoring and data security. However, it introduces
challenges such as high processing demands, latency, and cyber-
security risks. Combining DTs with blockchain technology can
help mitigate tampering concerns. Nevertheless, regulatory
and privacy issues persist, particularly in global applications.
Future advances may leverage edge computing to reduce latency,
enabling a more efﬁcient and secure DT-blockchain synergy for
optimized battery diagnostics and management.
7. Challenges and Future Directions
7.1. Energy Density, Fast Charging, and Safety Expectations
The shift to EVs increases the demand for higher energy density,
fast charging, and stringent safety in battery technologies. Key
targets include achieving 80% charge within 3C or 4C rates,
necessary for quick launch and sustained cruise in electric pro-
pulsion.[169,170] Safety remains critical, requiring energy density
improvements without compromising protection, as battery
safety directly impacts user and property security.[171]

sities and enhanced safety but require further research and

7.2. Advanced Sensing, Monitoring, and Data-Driven Modeling
Accurate sensing and state estimation are pivotal in optimizing
battery performance, as the internal states in EV batteries are
challenging to monitor directly due to the battery’s closed struc-
ture. Current methods rely heavily on estimation algorithms and
parameter identiﬁcation, but these often introduce errors and
lack precision.[172,174] Advanced sensors, like ﬁber-optic sensors,
have shown promise by enabling in situ monitoring of internal
battery strain and temperature in lithium-ion battery cells.[175,176]
New sensing technologies, such as ultrasonic transmission
probes and piezoelectric sensors, are increasingly used for
SoC and SoH estimation, enhancing accuracy beyond traditional
methods.[177,178] Additionally, displacement sensors are utilized
for detecting SoC imbalances by monitoring battery swelling,
contributing to better charge management.[179]
Combining diverse sensor data through multisensor fusion
technology is a future direction that aims to deliver real-time
and robust insights into the battery’s internal state, ultimately
improving BMS accuracy. This advanced sensing approach ena-
bles more precise fault diagnosis, health diagnostics, and overall
system robustness.[180]
7.3. Thermal Management and Aging Behavior Analysis
An effective battery management requires accurate modeling
that accounts for aging and operational stressors. Conven-
tional models like ECMs lack chemical detail and fail to capture
the complex electrochemical interactions within batteries.[181]
Physics-based models that consider electrochemical processes
offer greater ﬁdelity and provide valuable insights into aging
mechanisms, although these models face challenges in compu-
tational demands and robustness in real-world scenarios.[182]
A key focus in recent research is the development of models
that capture battery aging, including factors like capacity fade,
resistance increase, and memory effects from repetitive charging
cycles. Aging accelerates with factors like high temperatures and
cycling intensity, requiring models that adapt over a battery’s life-
cycle.[180] The data-driven approaches for modeling, while useful,
face robustness issues in varying real-world conditions, necessi-
tating comprehensive datasets that cover aging under diverse
conditions. The model simpliﬁcation and reduction are also crit-
ical, as they balance complexity with available computational
resources, making real-time applications more feasible.[183]
Lifecycle modeling further integrates these aspects by focus-
ing on long-term battery performance and predicting end-of-life
parameters. Improved lifecycle models will not only enhance
state estimation but also inform lifecycle management strategies,
making batteries more reliable across diverse applications
and extending their operational life in EVs and secondary
applications.[184]
7.4. Fault Diagnosis, Health Management, and Security
Fault diagnosis in BMS systems traditionally relies on threshold-
based methods for detecting over-voltage, over-current, and over-
temperature issues. While useful, these methods lack depth in
fault tracking and early warning, limiting their effectiveness
for managing complex issues like thermal and sensor faults.
This limitation can hinder the effectiveness of BMS in ensuring
battery safety and reliability. Advanced diagnostic approaches
have been developed to address these challenges. For instance,
a residual statistics-based method has been proposed for current
sensor fault diagnosis in LIBs, enhancing detection capabilities
beyond simple threshold methods.[185] Additionally, integrating
level shift anomaly detection has shown promise in accurately
identifying temperature faults in LIBs, providing faster and more
reliable fault diagnosis compared to traditional methods.[186]
Future improvements will leverage AI-driven techniques to
enhance fault detection, traceability, and prediction, supporting
advanced diagnostics across thermal, electrical, and sensor-
related faults.[187]
Battery aging impacts capacity and resistance, complicating
SoH and SoC accuracy. Effective health management must adapt
real-time monitoring to mitigate overheating, optimize charging,
and extend battery lifespan.[188,189] Security concerns are increas-
ing as cell performance variability, temperature shifts, and envi-
ronmental factors introduce risks like short circuits, electrolyte
decomposition, and ﬁre hazards. To manage these, BMS will
integrate protections, automated responses, and critical parame-
ter monitoring. These advancements in fault diagnosis, health
management, and security will foster more resilient, adaptive
BMS systems, improving battery safety, lifespan, and operational
reliability.
7.5. Sustainability: Recycling, Reuse, and Disposal
As the volume of spent LIBs grows, establishing efﬁcient recy-
cling, reuse, and disposal systems becomes increasingly critical.
Current recycling practices are limited, creating environmental
concerns due to hazardous waste classiﬁcation and potential
risks from improper disposal, including explosions, pollution,
and cleanup costs. Developing comprehensive systems for
battery collection and environmentally responsible recycling is
essential to reduce the ecological impact.
Battery reuse offers additional sustainability beneﬁts by
extending the life of retired batteries in secondary applications
like ESS. However, these applications require robust BMS algo-
rithms that can adapt to the aged battery’s changing electrochem-
ical properties.[190] Many existing BMS algorithms rely on
laboratory-tested data, which may not accurately represent the
characteristics of older batteries, leading to safety concerns.
To improve battery sustainability, recycling efforts should
focus on reclaiming valuable materials such as copper, alumi-
num, and cobalt, which are increasingly costly to extract.

7.6. Intergration of 5G and Big Data in BMS
The integration of 5G and Big Data into BMS advances real-time
data handling, monitoring, and diagnostics, enabling smarter
systems. The rise of V2G and 5G networks requires expanded
BMS bandwidth for rapid data transmission, real-time monitor-
ing, and fault detection.[192] Big Data platforms and cloud com-
puting enhance algorithm accuracy for SoH and SoC estimation.
Cloud-based BMS and digital twins address data recording,
processing limitations, and enable adaptive management in real
time. The 5G infrastructure also facilitates data sharing across
EVs, promoting inter-vehicle energy sharing and predictive
maintenance.[193,194] Additionally, 5G-enabled V2V, V2H, and
V2G interactions support a comprehensive network approach
connecting EVs with broader smart grids.[195,196]
8. Conclusion
The advancement of BMS is central to the development of efﬁ-
cient, safe, and sustainable EVs. This review has systematically
covered state-of-the-art battery technologies, BMS functionalities,
and the integration of emerging technologies such as AI, cloud
computing, and blockchain. Additionally, challenges such as
thermal management, state estimation, fault diagnosis, and recy-
cling were discussed, alongside innovative solutions aimed at
overcoming these barriers. Technological advancements have
signiﬁcantly improved SoC estimation accuracy. Current meth-
ods now achieve less than 1% MAE, a substantial improvement
over earlier techniques with rates up to 5%. This progress not
only enhances BMS reliability but also indicates potential for fur-
ther advancements as technologies evolve. To continue enhanc-
ing BMS performance, critical research gaps must be addressed,
particularly in developing robust state estimation techniques that
could further lower MAE rates. The integration of V2G and V2H
systems will also enhance energy management capabilities.
Additionally, exploring hybrid cooling systems and advanced
safety measures will be crucial for ensuring the reliability and
longevity of LIBs. Collaborative efforts in data sharing, standard-
ization, and security are essential for creating interconnected
vehicular ecosystems. By leveraging interdisciplinary approaches
and closing current technological gaps, BMS technologies can
signiﬁcantly enhance EV performance, contributing to the global
transition toward a sustainable energy future. Continued
innovation is essential for meeting the increasing demands of
electriﬁcation while supporting environmental goals and energy
resilience.
